result.markdown: --- title: "Session 3 — Categorical Outcomes" subtitle: "Goodness of fit · chi-square for 2 x 2 and larger tables · expected counts · Fisher · McNemar · effect sizes and residuals · Lab 3" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are {#where-we-are} ::: {.incremental} - Sessions 1–2: describe, check, and the assumptions behind the tests - Today: the outcome is a **category** (yes/no, or several groups) - By the end you can: - test one proportion against an expected value - choose between **chi-square** and **Fisher's exact** from the **expected** counts - test a **paired** yes/no outcome with **McNemar** - report a **risk difference**, **odds ratio** or **Cramér's V**, and find **which cells** drive a result ::: # Topic 1 — One group {#topic-1-one-group background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Goodness of fit: is the split what we expected? {#goodness-of-fit-is-the-split-what-we-expected} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} observed <- table(p$ever_screened_for_bp) observed ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` no yes 202 429 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} chisq.test(observed, p = c(0.5, 0.5)) # expected: half screened, half not ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Chi-squared test for given probabilities data: observed X-squared = 81.662, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: ## Better: estimate the proportion with its CI {#better-estimate-the-proportion-with-its-ci} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} binom.test(sum(p$ever_screened_for_bp == "yes"), nrow(p))$conf.int ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.6419014 0.7161517 attr(,"conf.level") [1] 0.95 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.eq} "68.0% of adults had ever been screened for blood pressure (95% CI 64.2 to 71.6%)." ::: - The test only says "not 50%"; the **proportion and its CI** say **how many** were screened - Use goodness of fit when the expected split is a real benchmark (a census, a target, a genetic ratio) # Topic 2 — Two groups, two outcomes: the 2 x 2 table {#topic-2-two-groups-two-outcomes-the-2-x-2-table background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Diabetes in women and men {#diabetes-in-women-and-men} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} t_sex <- table(p$sex_of_participants, p$past_history_of_diabetes) t_sex ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` no yes female 321 14 male 283 13 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} chisq.test(t_sex, correct = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pearson's Chi-squared test data: t_sex X-squared = 0.017372, df = 1, p-value = 0.8951 ``` ::: ::: ## The assumption is about **expected** counts {#the-assumption-is-about-expected-counts} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(chisq.test(t_sex)$expected, 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` no yes female 320.7 14.3 male 283.3 12.7 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - Expected count = row total × column total / grand total: what the table would hold if there were **no** association - Chi-square is reliable when **at least 80%** of expected counts are **≥ 5** and **none is below 1** (Cochran's rule) - In a **2 × 2** table: if **any** expected count is below 5, use **Fisher's exact test** - The **observed** counts can be small; it is the **expected** counts that matter ::: ## Report the effect, not only p {#report-the-effect-not-only-p} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prop.test(t_sex[, "yes"], rowSums(t_sex))$conf.int * 100 # difference in % (women − men) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -3.594384 3.168809 attr(,"conf.level") [1] 0.95 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.eq} "A past history of diabetes was reported by 4.2% of women and 4.4% of men (difference -0.2 percentage points, 95% CI -3.6 to 3.2; p = 0.895)." ::: - **Risk difference** (percentage points) is the easiest to read; the **odds ratio** suits case-control data and regression - The CI includes 0: no evidence of a difference, and differences of a few points either way are still possible ## When an expected count is small: Fisher {#when-an-expected-count-is-small-fisher} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} t_htn <- table(hypertension = p$past_history_of_hypertension, diabetes = p$past_history_of_diabetes) t_htn ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` diabetes hypertension no yes no 553 17 yes 51 10 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} round(chisq.test(t_htn)$expected, 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` diabetes hypertension no yes no 545.6 24.4 yes 58.4 2.6 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} broom::tidy(fisher.test(t_htn)) |> select(estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 4 estimate conf.low conf.high p.value 1 6.34 2.46 15.6 0.0000786 ``` ::: ::: ## Reading Fisher's result {#reading-fishers-result} ::: {.eq} "Diabetes was more common in adults with a past history of hypertension: 16.4% vs 3.0% (odds ratio 6.3, 95% CI 2.5 to 15.6; Fisher's exact test, p < 0.001)." ::: ::: {.incremental} - An expected count of 2.6 triggers R's warning *"Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect"*: that is the cue for Fisher - The CI is **wide** (2.5 to 15.6) because only 10 adults have both conditions: report it, do not hide it - This is an **association**, not proof that one causes the other ::: ## Yates' correction {#yates-correction} ::: {.incremental} - `chisq.test()` on a 2 × 2 table applies **Yates' continuity correction** by default (`correct = TRUE`): it subtracts 0.5 from each |observed − expected| - It makes the test **conservative** (p a little too large) - With adequate expected counts, `correct = FALSE` is fine; with small ones, use **Fisher** rather than relying on Yates - Whatever you choose, **say which** in the methods ::: # Topic 3 — Larger tables {#topic-3-larger-tables background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Marital status and wealth (3 x 5) {#marital-status-and-wealth-3-x-5} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x_mw <- chisq.test(table(p$marital_status_of_participants, p$wealth_index_of_participants)) x_mw ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pearson's Chi-squared test data: table(p$marital_status_of_participants, p$wealth_index_of_participants) X-squared = 29.05, df = 8, p-value = 0.0003108 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} round(x_mw$expected, 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` poorest poorer middle richer richest never married 5.3 7.9 9.7 11.0 10.1 currently married 65.2 96.9 119.2 135.5 124.3 formerly/ever married 5.5 8.2 10.1 11.5 10.6 ``` ::: ::: ## A significant table: **where** is the difference? {#a-significant-table-where-is-the-difference} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(x_mw$stdres, 1) # standardised residuals: beyond ±2 = a cell that stands out ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` poorest poorer middle richer richest never married 0.8 -2.0 -0.3 1.4 0.0 currently married -2.5 -1.2 0.5 0.9 1.5 formerly/ever married 2.6 3.5 -0.4 -2.7 -2.0 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cramers_v(table(p$marital_status_of_participants, p$wealth_index_of_participants)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Cramer's V (adj.) | 95% CI -------------------------------- 0.13 | [0.01, 1.00] - One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00]. ``` ::: ::: - **Formerly married** adults (mostly widowed) are **over**-represented among the poorest and poorer (+2.6, +3.5) and **under**-represented among the richer (-2.7); the currently married show the mirror image - Cramér's V = 0.13: a **weak** association, though clearly not chance ## If expected counts are too small: Monte Carlo {#if-expected-counts-are-too-small-monte-carlo} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2026) chisq.test(table(p$marital_status_of_participants, p$wealth_index_of_participants), simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 10000)$p.value ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.00049995 ``` ::: ::: - Simulates tables with the same margins: the p-value no longer relies on large expected counts - The smallest possible p is 1 / (B + 1): increase **B** for small p-values; set a **seed** so the result can be reproduced - Alternative for small tables: `fisher.test()`, which also handles r × c tables (add `simulate.p.value = TRUE` when the table is large) # Topic 4 — Paired yes/no outcomes {#topic-4-paired-yesno-outcomes background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Foot pain before and after: McNemar {#foot-pain-before-and-after-mcnemar} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} t_pain <- table(before = p$pain_foot_bfr, after = p$pain_foot_aftr) t_pain ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` after before No Yes No 398 17 Yes 104 112 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mcnemar.test(t_pain) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` McNemar's Chi-squared test with continuity correction data: t_pain McNemar's chi-squared = 61.124, df = 1, p-value = 5.359e-15 ``` ::: ::: ## Only the people who **changed** count {#only-the-people-who-changed-count} ::: {.incremental} - 17 adults went from no pain to pain; 104 from pain to no pain - McNemar compares these two **discordant** cells; the 510 who did not change carry no information about change - Few discordant pairs (under about 25)? Use the **exact** McNemar test: `exact2x2::mcnemar.exact(t_pain)` (load the package with `library(exact2x2)` first) ::: ::: {.eq} "Foot pain was reported by 34.2% of adults before and 20.4% after the foot-care programme (104 improved, 17 developed pain; McNemar test, p < 0.001)." ::: ## Which test for a category outcome? {#which-test-for-a-category-outcome} | Situation | Test | Effect to report | |---|---|---| | One proportion vs a benchmark | binomial test / goodness of fit | proportion (95% CI) | | 2 × 2, all expected ≥ 5 | chi-square | risk difference or odds ratio (95% CI) | | 2 × 2, any expected < 5 | Fisher's exact | odds ratio (95% CI) | | r × c, ≥ 80% expected ≥ 5, none < 1 | chi-square + residuals | Cramér's V; which cells | | r × c, small expected counts | Monte Carlo or Fisher | Cramér's V | | Paired yes/no | McNemar (exact if few changes) | % before and after | ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 3 {#switch-to-r-lab-3 .lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `stats-workshop/labs/lab3_categorical.R` - a proportion with its 95% CI - a 2 × 2 table: expected counts first, then chi-square or Fisher - risk difference and odds ratio, in a sentence - a larger table: residuals and Cramér's V - McNemar for before-and-after ::: **Time:** 35 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {#self-check-quiz-15 .smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t3q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="il46q3.9z6si3" data-show="Q2hpLXNxdWFyZSB0ZXN0LCBiZWNhdXNlIHRoZSBydWxlIGlzIGFib3V0IGV4cGVjdGVkIGNv dW50cw==" data-explain="VGhlIGNoaS1zcXVhcmUgYXBwcm94aW1hdGlvbiBkZXBlbmRzIG9uIHRoZSBleHBlY3RlZCBj b3VudHMgKHJvdyB0b3RhbCB4IGNvbHVtbiB0b3RhbCAvIGdyYW5kIHRvdGFsKSwgbm90IHRo ZSBvYnNlcnZlZCBvbmVzLiBXaXRoIGV2ZXJ5IGV4cGVjdGVkIGNvdW50IGFib3ZlIDUsIGNo aS1zcXVhcmUgaXMgZmluZS4="} A 2 x 2 table has an observed count of 2 in one cell, but all four expected counts are above 10. Which test fits? - Fisher's exact test, because one observed count is small - McNemar test, because the table has a very small cell in it - Chi-square test, because the rule is about expected counts - No test at all, because the table is far too unbalanced ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {#self-check-quiz-25 .smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t3q2" data-type="fill" data-hashes="il4jyt.9z76zh,ufpfen.uziu93" data-show="Mw==" data-explain="Q29jaHJhbidzIHJ1bGU6IGF0IGxlYXN0IDgwJSBvZiBleHBlY3RlZCBjb3VudHMgbXVzdCBi ZSA1IG9yIG1vcmUgKGFuZCBub25lIGJlbG93IDEpLiAyMCUgb2YgMTUgY2VsbHMgaXMgMy4="} In a 3 x 5 table (15 cells), at most how many expected counts may be below 5 for chi-square to be acceptable by Cochran's rule? (Give a whole number.) ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {#self-check-quiz-35 .smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t3q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="il4x7g.9z7lgs" data-show="QSB3ZWFrIGJ1dCByZWFsIGFzc29jaWF0aW9uOyByZXNpZHVhbHMgc2hvdyB3aGljaCBjZWxs cw==" data-explain="QSBzbWFsbCBwIHNheXMgdGhlIHBhdHRlcm4gaXMgdW5saWtlbHkgdG8gYmUgY2hhbmNlOyBW IHNheXMgaXQgaXMgd2Vhay4gVGhlIHN0YW5kYXJkaXNlZCByZXNpZHVhbHMgc2hvdyB3aGVy ZSBpdCBjb21lcyBmcm9tLiBBbiBhc3NvY2lhdGlvbiBpbiBzdXJ2ZXkgZGF0YSBkb2VzIG5v dCBzaG93IGNhdXNlLg=="} A chi-square test on marital status by wealth gives p < 0.001 and Cramér's V = 0.13. What is the best summary? - A strong association between marital status and wealth - A weak but real association; residuals show which cells - No association at all, since a V below 0.3 means none - Wealth is caused by marital status in this population group ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {#self-check-quiz-45 .smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t3q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="il5ag6.9z7zy6" data-show="T25seSB0aGUgcGVvcGxlIHdob3NlIGFuc3dlciBjaGFuZ2VkIGluIGVpdGhlciBkaXJlY3Rp b24=" data-explain="TWNOZW1hciBjb21wYXJlcyB0aGUgdHdvIGRpc2NvcmRhbnQgY2VsbHMgKG5vIHRvIHllcywg eWVzIHRvIG5vKS4gUGVvcGxlIHdobyBkaWQgbm90IGNoYW5nZSBjYXJyeSBubyBpbmZvcm1h dGlvbiBhYm91dCBjaGFuZ2Uu"} Which part of a before-and-after yes/no table does the McNemar test use? - All four cells of the table, weighted equally by their counts - Only the people whose answer stayed the same at both visits - Only the people whose answer changed in either direction - Only the row and column totals of the whole before-after table ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {#self-check-quiz-55 .smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t3q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="il5now.9z8efk" data-show="VGhhdCBmZXcgYWR1bHRzIGFyZSBpbiB0aGUgY2VsbCB3aXRoIGJvdGggY29uZGl0aW9ucw==" data-explain="T25seSAxMCBhZHVsdHMgaGFkIGJvdGggaHlwZXJ0ZW5zaW9uIGFuZCBkaWFiZXRlczsgZmV3 IGV2ZW50cyBtYWtlIHRoZSBlc3RpbWF0ZSBpbXByZWNpc2UuIFRoZSBpbnRlcnZhbCBleGNs dWRlcyAxLCBzbyB0aGUgYXNzb2NpYXRpb24gaXMgdW5saWtlbHkgdG8gYmUgY2hhbmNlLCBi dXQgaXRzIHNpemUgaXMgdW5jZXJ0YWluLg=="} Fisher's test gives an odds ratio of 6.3 with a 95% CI from 2.5 to 15.6. What does the wide interval mainly reflect? - That the true odds ratio is most likely close to 9 - That Fisher's exact test gives intervals this wide by design - That the p-value is likely above 0.05 for this comparison - That few adults are in the cell with both conditions ::: ## Score and take-home {#score-and-take-home} **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - Check **expected** counts: chi-square if ≥ 80% are ≥ 5 and none < 1; Fisher for a 2 × 2 with any below 5 - Report **proportions** and an **effect** (risk difference, odds ratio, Cramér's V) with a 95% CI - A significant larger table: the **residuals** say where - Paired yes/no: **McNemar**, driven by the people who changed ::: **Next:** Session 4: comparing two groups on a number

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
